problem: Prior zero-shot ObjectNav methods mainly rank candidate frontiers/regions to decide where to go next, so repeated rescoring of nearby frontiers can keep the robot stuck in a semantically unsuitable context and waste the action budget. Search persistence itself is not treated as a decision.
motivation: ObjectNav is a long-horizon decision problem under partial observability with a finite budget. Continuing and leaving are asymmetric choices: uncertainty should not trigger costly relocation, but clear evidence of a wrong context should. The paper therefore separates the decision to leave from the choice of destination.
key_idea: An LLM supervisor with an asymmetric context gate decides between continuing receding-horizon exploration and relocating to another graph-reachable frontier cluster, and it compares candidate clusters only after accumulated object evidence clearly conflicts with the target.
insight: Gains come from deciding when to leave the current region rather than only from better frontier scoring. In the HM3D-v2 ablation, removing the relocation gate drops SR from 87.6 to 82.1 and SPL from 52.7 to 39.9, and step-limit failures rise from 5.0% to 9.7%. Removing TSP ordering as well drops SPL further to 29.2, so global ordering and relocation are complementary, mainly by reducing budget exhaustion and path inflation.
method: Persistent 3D object clusters: semantic labels are projected with depth into a voxel map, and connected same-label voxels form clusters (label, voxel support, center, bounds), which suppresses frame-level noise and keeps evidence after objects leave view.

Frontier decision graph and cluster graph: frontiers are nodes on a topological map with path-length edge costs. Frontiers connected by paths of cost ≤ρc=25 are merged into clusters, so wall-separated frontiers stay apart. Cluster edges reuse least-cost paths, and the frontier nearest the robot is the relocation waypoint.

Geometric pre-ranking and semantic attachment: clusters are ranked by U_geo = n(1+η r)/(1+d) and the top K=10 go to the supervisor. Each carries nearby object labels and supports within 10 m, and the robot-local context is also given.

Context-gated LLM supervisor: the LLM gets only label/support text, not images, and outputs JSON. It continues exploring unless local objects clearly conflict with the target's expected context; only then does it choose a relocation cluster by compatibility and distance. Invalid output falls back to exploration, rate limiting applies, and an active relocation is not interrupted.

Receding-horizon TSP exploration: the frontier visiting order is approximated by an open TSP, and only the first frontier is executed before replanning. A nearby frontier within 5 m overrides it if the first leg is more than twice as long.

Target gate and mission execution: a target cluster needs ≥10 voxels, ≥3 supporting observations and ≤5 consecutive misses, plus navigation verification. The camera turns toward the cluster and gets a fresh observation before STOP, and failed verification returns control to the supervisor. All missions share one waypoint executor.

setting.backbone: LLM supervisor (model not named in text, frozen, prompted with JSON action contract) + Habitat semantic observations / Mask2Former (real world) + classical mapping, TSP and planning
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D plus ground-truth semantic observations in Habitat, 640x480, 79° HFOV; panoramic RGB + LiDAR in the real world
setting.action_space: waypoint missions (explore / relocate / nav-to-object) executed via discrete FORWARD, TURN 30° L/R, STOP; 500-action limit
setting.privileged: Habitat semantic observations are used as the perception input (simulator semantic sensor); real world uses a prebuilt point-cloud map for localization

numbers.extra: complete val list; cross-paper baselines differ in success distance/protocol; own success radius 1.0 m

numbers.backbone: LLM supervisor disabled for relocation; TSP retained

numbers_note: Splits are labelled 'val' as the paper uses validation sets; HM3D-v1 and v2 are both mapped to HM3D-ObjNav. Other numbers were figure-only.
results: On complete unfiltered validation sets, SOR-Nav gets SR/SPL of 66.1/36.9 (HM3D-v1), 87.6/52.7 (HM3D-v2) and 61.8/38.5 (MP3D). This beats the strongest listed baselines (ApexNav 59.6/33.0 and SysNav 63.7/30.5 on HM3D-v1; SysNav 80.8/37.2 on HM3D-v2 and 50.7/18.1 on MP3D). A real-robot run finding three targets in sequence succeeded qualitatively.
limitations: Baseline numbers come from the SysNav table and use different success-distance and evaluation conventions, so the comparison is not controlled; Habitat uses semantic sensor inputs.
Multi-floor cases (58.7% of HM3D-v1 and 51.3% of MP3D failures) and long-distance search remain weak; the ablation does not isolate every representation component.
The real-world result is a single qualitative three-target demo, not a statistical benchmark, and the LLM adds latency and depends on rate limiting.
